models.summary: The cost of one person's privacy is the sum of three parts over 26 indicators in five groups: citizenship, social contact, finance, health and personal assets. The expected income sums a coefficient times each indicator's return. Ten citizenship indicators, hard to measure, take their coefficients from the analytic hierarchy process, whose consistency ratio passes below 0.1 and whose weights are printed. The other sixteen are treated as intangible assets and valued by the present-value method, with coefficients from a gradient boosting tree, each coefficient the negative gradient over the curvature plus a penalty. The risk value uses the coefficient of variation, deviation over expected value, and reuses the hierarchy weights as risk factors. The relatedness value follows an S-shaped Gaussian of the correlation, with parameters by maximum likelihood, so two people with equal income and equal risk can still differ in cost.

models.section: IV and V Pricing, elasticity and dynamics
models.summary: The selling price is the privacy cost plus a profit, and the margin is capped at 30 percent by analogy with ordinary goods. Demand elasticity is the relative change in quantity over the relative change in price, treated as positive though it is negative, and it falls through three life-cycle stages: flexible in growth, small or fixed at maturity, and possibly zero in decline. Because expectations of return rise as privacy awareness spreads, the 26 risk factors stop being constants and become functions of time. For total assets the fitted form is a decaying exponential with an R-square of 0.9779, and the same fit is applied to the other indicators and substituted into the risk-value formula. Generational differences enter by scaling the expected value with consumption growth by age, from 19 to 63.

models.summary: A small-world network of 40 people represents a group. A share n will sell privacy for gain and the rest will not. A seller exposes the two neighbours and, with probability p, people who are not neighbours. Simulation shows that disclosure grows steadily worse as n and p rise, so people who never sell are drawn in as the market grows. The same group is then read as a prisoner's dilemma with four cases. Under the economic-man rule anyone willing to sell does sell, which harms even those who refuse, so the refusers sell too. Without intervention the group settles into a subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium that is not the best outcome, and limiting personal selling is the way out.

models.summary: A large leak cuts all three parts of the privacy value: businesses buy less so the expected return falls, people grow less willing to sell, and the relatedness value falls with the return, which can bring the trading market to a crisis. Over time the damage takes one of two shapes. If the buyers steer public opinion the effect has a long tail; if nobody controls the opinion it whips like a bullwhip. The bullwhip can be held down, and as such events multiply each one hurts less, so the overall impact rises and then falls. The agency's payment is the value of the information plus the further losses, computed by a parametric actuarial model from insurance. A sensitivity check reweights the 26 indicators from a 50-person survey, drops 3 invalid groups, reprices the 500 simulated people, and reports no significant difference by an independent-samples test.
